description: We are looking for motivated and passionate teammates who are interested in space, agriculture, NASA data, and technology. Good English communication skills are essential, as team collaboration and discussions will be conducted in English. Experience in coding, AI/ML, data analysis, or design is a plus. Let's work together to build an innovative solution!
summary: Farmers worldwide face shifting temperatures, unpredictable rainfall, water shortages, and declining soil health — yet choosing a new crop rotation is hard because a crop that helps in one place may fail in another. Project Orbit & Furrow is a decision-support tool that brings NASA Earth observations down to the field level. Farmers locate their field and the tool retrieves SMAP soil moisture plus NASA POWER climate signals (temperature, precipitation, evapotranspiration, frost, vegetation stress) over a three-year window. A dashboard highlights water deficits, frost risk, and stress days. Farmers then drag six priority sliders — water, soil health, income, risk reduction, nitrogen fixation, pest disruption — and a transparent rule-based engine ranks three rotation strategies: their current rotation, a cover-crop alternative, and a drought-tolerant diversified rotation. Each strategy shows per-dimension scores, evidence, benefits, risks, and information gaps for local review. The engine adjusts weights when satellite data shows water deficit or stress. The tool is intentionally explainable — no black box — and is built to support, not replace, local farmer judgment and agronomist expertise.
details:
What it does and how it works

Orbit & Furrow is a web-based decision-support tool that walks a farmer through four steps:

  1. Locate the field — Enter latitude/longitude or pick one of six preset farms spanning continents (Iowa Corn Belt, Punjab wheat-rice, NSW Australia, Nakuru Kenya, Andalusia Spain, Saskatchewan Canada).
  2. Review field conditions — The tool fetches a synthetic SMAP soil moisture and NASA POWER climate series for that point: surface and root-zone soil moisture, 2m air temperature, daily minimum temperature (frost signal), precipitation, evapotranspiration, and NDVI proxy over the past three years. A dashboard surfaces four stat cards, a 12-month seasonal cycle chart, a 3-year water-balance bar chart, and auto-detected field notes (water deficit, frost risk, vegetation-stress days).
  3. Set priorities — Six sliders from 0–5 capture what matters most to the farmer: water conservation, soil health, income potential, weather/pest risk reduction, biological nitrogen fixation, and pest-cycle disruption.
  4. Compare three rotation strategies — The current rotation (corn → soybean) plus two alternatives: a winter cover-crop rotation (corn → winter rye → soybean → hairy vetch) and a drought-tolerant diversified rotation (sorghum → cowpea → sunflower). Each card shows an overall 0–100 score, per-dimension progress bars, a recommendation tag, and expandable sections for supporting evidence, benefits, risks to review locally, and information gaps.

Benefits

  • Explainable, not black-box: A rule-based scoring engine averages per-crop agronomic attributes (water need, nitrogen-fixing, root depth, erosion reduction, organic matter, drought/frost tolerance, market value, pest disruption) and weights them by farmer priorities. Every score can be traced back to a specific crop attribute.
  • Climate-aware: The engine reads the satellite record and boosts the effective weight of water conservation in water-deficit years, and risk reduction in high-frost or high-stress years. The same priorities produce different recommendations in Iowa versus Punjab.
  • Farmer-centered: Plain language, no jargon, mobile-responsive, expandable evidence instead of a wall of text.
  • Honest about uncertainty: Every rotation card lists explicit risks and information gaps that need local agronomist review.

Intended impact

Help farmers make rotation choices that conserve water, build soil organic matter, reduce erosion, disrupt pest cycles, and strengthen resilience to drought, frost, and shifting rainfall — while keeping the decision in human hands. The tool is explicitly designed to support, not replace, farmer judgment and local extension expertise.

Tools, languages, and software

  • Framework: Next.js 16 (App Router) with TypeScript 5
  • Styling: Tailwind CSS 4 with shadcn/ui (New York style) + Lucide icons
  • Charts: Recharts
  • Toasts: Sonner
  • NASA datasets emulated: SMAP (SPL4SMAU soil moisture, ~9 km grid) and NASA POWER (T2M, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, EVLAND on 0.5° grid). The MVP uses deterministic synthetic series calibrated to realistic climate-zone patterns so the demo runs anywhere without API keys; the generateFieldConditions() function is the single swap point for live NASA POWER and SMAP API integration post-hackathon.

How the project is creative

  • Bridges orbital data and field-level decisions — Most NASA ag tools stop at the dashboard. Orbit & Furrow goes one step further: it translates satellite signals into ranked rotation strategies with explicit trade-offs.
  • Climate-adjusted weighting — The engine doesn't just score rotations; it re-weights the farmer's own priorities based on what the satellite record shows is happening locally. A water-deficit year pushes water and risk-reduction weights up automatically.
  • Twelve-crop library with nine agronomic attributes per crop — Each crop carries water need, N-fixing flag, root depth, erosion reduction, organic matter contribution, drought and frost tolerance, market value, pest disruption, and season length. The library is transparent and easy to extend.
  • Three explicit strategies including the current rotation — Farmers see their existing practice scored alongside alternatives, not just recommendations out of context.

Factors the team considered

  • Farmer literacy and access: No login, no install, works on mobile, plain-language explanations of evapotranspiration, soil moisture, NDVI, and water balance.
  • Local validity: Every rotation card lists risks and information gaps that require local agronomist review (seed availability, equipment fit, market depth, soil-type interaction, termination timing).
  • Reproducibility: Synthetic series are deterministic per lat/lon so the same farm always produces the same data — important for demo reproducibility and for future comparison against real NASA API output.
  • Scalability: The architecture supports adding ECOSTRESS (land-surface temperature), GPM (precipitation), GRACE (groundwater trends), Landsat/MODIS (NDVI), and SRTM (elevation/slope) by extending generateFieldConditions() — no UI changes needed.
  • Honest MVP scope: The tool is a starting point for discussion, not a prescription. The disclaimer is repeated in the UI and footer.
